newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS- Wilcon optimistic as sets extra div.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS- Wilcon optimistic as sets extra div.

text.p: Housebuilder Wilson (Connolly) Holdings Plc on Tuesday pledged 10 million pounds($16 million) to give its shareholders a special dividend and expressed optimism that British house prices would rise.
The company made its comments as it posted 1996 results showing a 17 percent increase in pretax profits to 26.4 million pounds.

Wilson (Connolly), which trades as Wilcon, said its planned cash distribution was in stark contrast to the industry trend which has been to raise funds from holders, with over 1.0 billion pounds raised across the sector since 1990.
After a poor 1995 market, and an only gradual revival of volumes in 1996, company chairman Lynn Wilson said solid foundations had now been laid for the future.
"I am encouraged by the hardening of prices in the south of England, which now shows signs of spreading to some other parts of the country," Wilson said.
Managing Director Ian Black said the 1997 housing market would be tested by the UK general election and related uncertainty.
"Although our reservation numbers are similar numerically to this time last year, our forward order book is more profitable and provides a platform for further growth in group profits."

Behind the 10 million pound special payback to shareholders, to be distributed in the form of a 5.0 pence per share special dividend, was Wilcon's withdrawal during last year from commercial property development.
The directors said the move had reduced working capital tied up in this activity by 11 million pounds.
Meanwhile, funds have also been pushed into new plots so that its year-end land bank of 17,400 plots is one of the longest in the industry, Wilcon added.
In 1996 it sold 4,150 houses, up from 3,870 in 1995, at an average price of 61,580 pounds, up from 59,600 a year ago.
Wilcon said it was continuing to expand its product range and was bringing in a new series of house types at the top end of its market segment.
Industry observers said a richer mix of higher price houses should help consolidate the company's profit margins at higher levels than those seen during the lean period of 1995 and early 1996.

Black said that a stark contrast in pretax margins between early 1996 (down to 5.9 percent) and the second half (up to 10.9 percent) meant the average for the year was only slightly higher at 8.7 percent than 1995's 8.4 percent.
Wilcon's share price advanced steadily after the results, despite a broadly weaker London market, and by 0945 GMT the shares were up 5.0 pence at 165 pence.
